Finding the Membrane

The pattern to recognize: a bright convex line a few millimeters deep, with repeating reverberation bands beneath it from the air column. Cricothyrotomy — Surgical, Percutaneous & Needle

Finding the Membrane

One drawing, four procedures: the membrane is the cricothyrotomy target, the 2nd–3rd ring interspace is the tracheostomy target, the same membrane is punctured cephalad for retrograde intubation, and this is the anatomy you mark pre-induction in a high-risk neck before a possible CICO.

Cricothyrotomy — Surgical, Percutaneous & Needle

Finding the Membrane

The schematic above tells you the order; this is what it looks like on a neck. Walk down the midline from the hyoid: the first soft gap is the thyrohyoid membrane — wrong. The second, between the thyroid cartilage and the cricoid ring, is the target. On a neck you cannot read, the vertical incision is what saves you, not the picture.

Cricothyrotomy — Surgical, Percutaneous & Needle

Needle Cricothyrotomy — And Why Exhalation Is the Whole Problem

If the chest does not come back down between insufflations, stop. Stacking breaths into a chest that cannot empty is how this technique kills people — and it is the reason a needle cricothyrotomy is a bridge, never the answer to a completely obstructed airway.

why-needle-cricothyrotomy-depends-on-the-upper-airway.svg

Retrograde Intubation

Stepwise Technique

The needle angles cephalad — the most commonly inverted detail in this procedure, precisely because cricothyrotomy, percutaneous tracheostomy and transtracheal blocks all angle the other way.

retrograde-intubation-wire-direction-shown-as-a-vertical-sch.svg

Chest Tube Placement (Tube Thoracostomy)

The Triangle of Safety

Pectoralis major in front, latissimus dorsi behind, the axilla above. Enter in the 4th–5th interspace just anterior to the mid-axillary line, over the top of the rib. The one refinement over the usual description: the lower edge follows the rib. A horizontal line drawn back from the nipple drifts about one space low by the time it reaches latissimus.

safe-triangle-on-real-anatomy.svg

Chest Tube Placement (Tube Thoracostomy)

The Triangle of Safety

The ribs climb toward the back, so a level line from the nipple crosses into a lower space as it goes. Below the lung, the costodiaphragmatic recess is pleura with no lung in it, and the spleen (on the right, the liver) sits just under the diaphragm beneath it. A low tube goes there.

why-the-lower-edge-follows-the-rib.svg

Finger Thoracostomy / Needle Decompression

Choosing the Site

Pectoralis major in front, latissimus dorsi behind, the axilla above. Enter in the 4th–5th interspace just anterior to the mid-axillary line, over the top of the rib. The one refinement over the usual description: the lower edge follows the rib. A horizontal line drawn back from the nipple drifts about one space low by the time it reaches latissimus.

Pericardiocentesis

Stepwise Technique

Blind or landmark-guided: enter just left of and below the xiphoid, pass under the costal margin at about 30° to the skin, and aim for the left shoulder, aspirating as you go; steepen only if the first pass returns no fluid. The needle meets the inferior surface of the heart, mostly right ventricle. With ultrasound, scan every window and use the one where the fluid is largest and closest.

Transcutaneous & Transvenous Pacing

Transcutaneous Pacing — Setup & Technique

Anterior pad over the left precordium, just left of the sternum (about V2–V3). Posterior pad on the left back, below the scapula and beside the spine. The current runs through the heart between them. Pad positions are drawn by hand on the engravings.

transcutaneous-pad-placement-anterior-posterior.svg

Transcutaneous & Transvenous Pacing

Confirming Capture — And Why False Capture Fools People

Both tracings have a spike before every wide deflection, and on a moving monitor they look alike. The difference is the discordant T wave and, decisively, whether there is a pulse wave beneath it — which is why you confirm with a femoral pulse, an arterial line, or bedside echo rather than the monitor alone.

true-capture-versus-false-capture-during-pacing.svg

Transcutaneous & Transvenous Pacing

Transvenous Pacing — Floating the Wire

If the ST elevation appears and then disappears, you have lost wall contact — that is not progress. Depth is only a sanity check: roughly 30–35 cm from a right IJ.

Symphysiotomy & Procedural Shoulder Dystocia Maneuvers

The Escalation Sequence

The ladder is drawn against the clock because teams consistently believe far less time has passed than actually has — which is why a scribe calls it out every 30 seconds. Note where the sequence ends up: working it through once takes roughly four minutes, so there is no spare time for repeating a maneuver that has already failed.

Escharotomy

Where the Lines Go — and the Two Nerves

Length is what fails, not placement: an incision that stops short of the joint or ends inside burned skin leaves the constriction where it is tightest. The two amber points are the only places the line deviates, and both are marked on the skin before cutting, because eschar hides the landmarks you would normally navigate by.

escharotomy-incision-map-anterior-view.svg

Central Line Placement Under Arrest Conditions

Femoral Technique During Active CPR

Find the ligament from bone: ASIS to pubic tubercle. Puncture 1–2 cm below it, just medial to the artery — which in arrest you find with the probe, not your fingers. Too low, in the crease, you are among the branches; too high, you are in the retroperitoneum.

femoral-vein-below-the-inguinal-ligament.svg

Intraosseous Access

Proximal Humerus — The One People Miss

Internal rotation and the 45° caudad angle are the two things that make this line work, and neither is visible once the drill is in your hand. A needle driven perpendicular to the skin travels medially through the head and into the glenohumeral joint — it will stand up convincingly, flush poorly, and infiltrate.

proximal-humerus-intraosseous-access-in-two-steps.svg

Intraosseous Access

Proximal Tibia — Adult and Pediatric

The tuberosity is the reference, not the target. Adult goes proximal to it; a child goes distal — opposite directions, for the one reason shown here. Getting them backwards in a child puts the needle through an open physis.

proximal-tibial-intraosseous-landmarks-anterior-view-of-the-.svg

Lateral Canthotomy

Technique

The tarsal plates are anchored to the lateral orbital rim by the two crura of the lateral canthal tendon. The canthotomy (1) only gets you to them; the pressure comes off when the inferior crus (2) is cut and the lower lid swings free. If it is still tight, take the superior crus.

lateral-canthotomy-on-the-tarsal-plates.svg

Pelvic Binder Placement

Why the Greater Trochanters

The binder closes the ring by rotating both halves of the pelvis around the femoral heads, so it has to sit at the greater trochanters, level with the symphysis — far lower than instinct says. At the iliac crests it squeezes above that axis and does nothing useful.

binder-level-trochanters-not-iliac-crests.svg

Resuscitative Endovascular Balloon Occlusion of the Aorta (REBOA)

The Zones — and the One You Never Occlude

Zone 1 buys the most pressure at the highest cost: every abdominal organ, both kidneys and the cord sit downstream. Zone 3 spares all of them. If the proximal pressure does not rise on inflation, the balloon is under-inflated, malpositioned — or the bleeding is above it.

the-three-reboa-aortic-zones.svg
